The presentation begins with a title slide displaying 'ACL 2023' in the top right corner. The main content starts with an introduction to text-to-image ambiguity, discussing how ambiguous prompts can lead to different interpretations of visual setups and emphasizing the need for frameworks to mitigate these ambiguities. It introduces two specific approaches: QA-TIED and VS-TIED.

The first approach, QA-TIED, involves using in-context learning for language models (LMs) to generate clarifying questions that resolve ambiguities by providing more context or details about the image. This is illustrated through examples where LMs are asked to clarify aspects like the girl's pink shirt versus her wearing it. The second approach, VS-TIED, focuses on generating multiple plausible visual setups based on the ambiguous prompt and evaluating them automatically against human evaluations to determine which setup best matches the original intent.

The presentation continues to elaborate on the VS-TIED method, showing bar charts comparing performance metrics across different datasets such as DALL-E Mega and OpenAI DALL-E. These charts illustrate the differences between various models like DALL-E 1, DALL-E 2, and Stable Diffusion, highlighting their accuracy rates for resolving ambiguities. The final part of this segment emphasizes the importance of automatic evaluation methods and provides references to further readings from the paper.

The conclusion section reiterates key points: studying ambiguities in Text-to-Image models, curating the Text-to-Image Ambiguity Benchmark (TAB), proposing frameworks to mitigate and evaluate ambiguities, and demonstrating the effectiveness of these frameworks through automated vs. manual evaluations. The consistent use of diagrams helps visualize the concepts being discussed throughout the slides.

The presentation concludes with a thank you message displayed within a blue speech bubble next to a cartoon character holding up three question marks. Below the character, there are images depicting different scenarios involving people interacting with objects, reinforcing the discussion on resolving ambiguities in text-to-image tasks. The page number '10' appears at the bottom center of the slide, indicating its position within the overall sequence of the presentation.

The presentation slide titled 'Attention as a Guide for Simultaneous Translation' features the authors Sara Papi, Matteo Negri, and Marco Turchi from the University of Trento. The slide discusses the challenges in simultaneous speech translation (SimulST) and introduces their solution called EDAtt (Encoder-Decoder Attention). It explains how attention mechanisms can be used to improve real-time speech translation by considering when to emit words based on audio frames. The slide includes visual representations of BLEU scores across different latency thresholds (AL/AL_CA) and emphasizes that EDAtt outperforms other strategies applied to offline models. Additionally, it highlights that EDAtt is the fastest strategy if we consider the actual elapsed time. Contact information for the authors and a QR code are also provided at the bottom right corner of the slide.\n\nThe slide transitions smoothly through various sections, maintaining consistency with blue text and icons throughout. The final section encourages viewers to read more about the results in their paper and provides contact details via email addresses, GitHub link, and Twitter handles. A large QR code labeled 'Scan me!' is prominently displayed, inviting further engagement or access to additional resources.

The video begins with a presentation slide titled 'Dialogue Summarization' by Shen Gao from Shandong University. It introduces the topic of summarizing dialogue using static and dynamic graph structures, featuring a red banner at the top displaying the title in white text. Below this, there is an image of a building labeled 'Shandong University,' followed by the subtitle 'Our Framework.' The main content area shows a flowchart illustrating the process of converting utterances into a summary through various steps including 'Static Graph Construction,' 'Dynamic Graph Construction,' and 'Static-Dynamic Graph Module.' Each step details specific components such as 'Discourse Parsing Graph,' 'Static Graph Fusion Module,' and 'Fusion Module,' explaining how different methods are used to generate summaries based on discourse relations like comment, clarification, acknowledgment, continuation, explanation, conditional, question-answer, alternation, question-elimination, result, background, narration, correction, parallel, and contrast.

The next segment focuses on the 'Static-Dynamic Graph Module,' detailing the conversion of discrete distances between utterances into vector space representations. This involves mathematical expressions for generating the adjacency matrix \(G^s\) and incorporating it with the relation matrix \(G^d\). The output embedding is then described as \(G^u = Conv(A \oplus G^s)\), where \(A\) represents the relation matrix of the dynamic graph and \(G^s\) denotes the adjacent matrix of the static graph. The importance of capturing the graph representation that captures the dialogue structure information in the generation is emphasized.

Following this, the focus shifts to the 'Summary Generator,' which incorporates the graph representation captured during the generation phase. The generated summary example provided is 'I got a ticket for concert C is going too.' The diagram illustrates the process involving a decoder with attention mechanisms (Feed Forward, Graph Attention, Dialogue Attention) and self-attention layers, leading to the output embedding. Mathematical equations describe how these processes integrate the graph representation into the final output.

The subsequent part highlights the 'Static-Dynamic Graph Module' again, emphasizing its role in integrating the adjacency matrices of static graphs with those derived from dynamic graphs via element-wise addition. The equation \(G^p = MHAtt(p^s, \{h_{1,1}, ..., h_{L_d, i}\) and \(G^q = MHAtt(p^g, \{g_1, ..., g_d\})\) illustrate how these matrices contribute to the fusion module's function. The key message here is about combining the adjacency matrices of static and dynamic graphs to capture the dialogue structure information effectively.

Finally, the video transitions to a thank you note section with a red background. At the top left corner, the text reads 'Data & Code' along with a GitHub link: https://github.com/Hannibal046/SDDS. A QR code is displayed prominently below this text. In the center, large bold letters spell out 'Thanks!' Above this central text, the name 'Shengao' appears, indicating the author or presenter. Below the 'Thanks!' text, smaller font size provides contact information: shengao@sdu.edu.cn. The overall design maintains consistency with previous slides, focusing on providing resources and acknowledgments related to the SDDS framework presented earlier.

The video begins with a title slide that reads 'Dual Cache for Neural Coreference Resolution' in large, bold letters. Below the title, there is additional text providing more context: 'Authors: Qiang Guo, Xiangkun Hu, Yue Zhang, Zheng Zeng, and Yuxuan Wang.' The background of this slide features logos from AWS, Tsinghua University, and the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL). At the bottom right corner, there is an image of a person holding a coffee mug.
Next, another title slide appears, displaying 'Coreference Resolution' at the top. This section introduces coreference resolution as identifying mentions within a text that refer to the same entity or concept. An example sentence is provided: 'I saw John talking to Maria. He was explaining something to her.' The words 'John,' 'Maria,' and 'her' are highlighted in red, indicating entities being referred to by pronouns.
Following this, a new slide titled 'Cache-based Coreference Resolution' explains how high-frequency entities can be referenced globally using caches. It includes two paragraphs describing the approach:
1. 'High-frequency entities such as "John" and "Maria" often appear multiple times in documents.' 2. 'These frequent entities should not need to be referenced locally each time they occur.'
An example table compares different methods on public benchmarks: - Column headers include 'Method,' 'Cache Size,' 'F1 Score,' and 'Time.' - Rows compare results between 'L-cache,' 'G-cache,' 'Dual cache,' and 'Unbound.' - Specific values like 'F1 Score = 0.84' and 'Time = 1.5s' under 'Dual cache' highlight its performance. - A note states: 'With training data, Dual cache outperforms baselines even without unbounded memory.'
A subsequent slide presents a graph comparing inference time versus F1 score across three datasets ('LitBank,' 'OnNotes,' and 'WikiCoref'). Two lines represent L-cache (blue) and G-cache (red), showing their performance relative to dual cache (green).
Another graph illustrates computation cost per million annotated characters (MAC) against dataset size. Three lines indicate costs for L-cache (blue), G-cache (red), and dual cache (green), emphasizing efficiency improvements.
A concluding slide lists key points about dual cache's advantages over single cache: - 'Dual Cache uses a local cache and a global cache to store local and global entities separately.' - 'Dual Cache outperforms single cache methods on public benchmarks.' - 'Dual Cache largely reduces cache misses.' - 'Dual Cache is the most cost-effective compared with single cache.'
The final frame displays the word 'Thanks,' expressing gratitude likely towards the audience or collaborators involved in the presentation.
Throughout these slides, the consistent presence of a small image of a person holding a coffee mug provides continuity and personal touch to the presentation.

The slide titled 'Revisiting Minimal Pair Paradigm' discusses the robustness of language model acceptability judgments to context length, structural match, and acceptability. It presents a comparison between two minimal pairs: "Many people were helping" vs. "No customer was having," with the latter being deemed unacceptable due to its lack of logical coherence. The slide also includes an example sentence about a documentary on cleaning the museum, highlighting how matched prefixes can affect LM performance. A graph shows the impact of different perturbations on model accuracy across various prefix types. The key takeaways emphasize that models are sensitive to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences and that MPP evaluations do not fully capture LMs' abstract knowledge.

The slide titled 'Compositional Generalization without Trees' introduces the concept of compositional generalization in semantic parsing. It explains that input tokens are tagged with multiset tags, and these tags correspond to the elements of a multiset. The slide emphasizes the importance of trees for deeper recursion and shows how input tokens are tagged as '*girl x1'.

The slide titled 'Why weakly supervised learning (WSL) works' introduces the topic with a heading in red text. It features two main sections: 'Recent WSL approaches' and 'Our recommendations.' The slide titled 'Neural Divide-and-Conquer Reasoning Framework' provides an in-depth look at the framework's components and their interactions. It includes a detailed diagram of the system architecture, highlighting various modules such as 'Visual Symbolic Inference,' 'System 1,' 'System 2,' 'Negation Operator,' and 'Conjunction Operator.' The text explains that System 1 performs perceptual calculation results on simple propositions from images, while System 2 decomposes complex reasoning into simple problems to construct the reasoning path. The slide titled 'Background' introduces the concept of watermarking in large language models (LLMs) and embedding-based services, emphasizing their exceptional performance in natural language understanding tasks. It highlights challenges such as model theft through backdoor attacks and the need for robust copyright protection mechanisms to prevent unauthorized use or leakage of intellectual property within these systems. The text explains that existing solutions are not applicable due to privacy concerns but suggests a new approach called EmbMarker, which aims to address these issues by incorporating watermarking techniques into EaaS platforms.

The next section labeled 'Existing Works' provides detailed information on various datasets used in experiments, including AG News, Enron Spam, MIND, and SST2, along with metrics like accuracy and detection performance using specific methods. This part emphasizes the importance of evaluating different approaches to ensure effective watermarking and reliable copyright verification in LLMs and EaaS platforms.

The final segment focuses on 'Experimental Results,' showcasing four scatter plots visualizing embeddings from different datasets: AG News, Enron Spam, MIND, and SST2. These plots illustrate how the data points align across different conditions, providing insights into the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to other state-of-the-art approaches. The results indicate significant improvements in terms of accuracy and detection performance, demonstrating the practical benefits of integrating watermarking into real-world applications involving large language models and embedded service providers.

The presentation concludes with a slide simply stating 'Thanks!' indicating the end of the presentation.

The slide titled 'Cross-lingual Performance Gap' presents a radar chart comparing the performance of different models across various datasets. The chart includes four categories: Matis, MGEOQuery, MSniper, MOveright, MCWQI, and MTOP. Each category is represented by a line on the radar chart, with numerical values indicating the model's performance in each dataset. The lines are color-coded to differentiate between various training methods or settings. At the bottom of the chart, there is an average score for each category, providing a comprehensive view of how well each model performs overall. This detailed visual representation helps in understanding the comparative effectiveness of different approaches within the context of cross-lingual semantic parsing tasks.

The next slide continues this analysis but focuses specifically on multilingual LLMs (Large Language Models). It highlights that Enc-Dec (mT5) outperforms previous work or achieves comparable results. Additionally, it emphasizes that pretraining on English can significantly boost performance on target NLs (Natural Languages), while Chinese transfer learning and monolingual training usually yield better outcomes than En -> En transfers. German has the smallest performance gap among these languages. FunQL generally outperforms other representations, although SQL still shows significant room for improvement. This section provides insights into the current state of language modeling techniques and their application in cross-lingual scenarios.

The following slides delve deeper into specific findings from the paper. They highlight that mT5 with monolingual training yields the best performance, especially compared to multilingual LLMs like Bloom. A comprehensive benchmark study was conducted on three representative types of multilingual language models. Results show that mT5 with monolingual training excels, particularly in handling cross-lingual semantic parsing tasks. However, notable gaps remain when transferring between multiple languages, emphasizing the ongoing challenges in achieving seamless multi-language integration in AI models.

The final sections conclude with practical applications and future directions. These include building XSemPLR as a unified benchmark for cross-lingual semantic parsing, conducting extensive studies on diverse language models, and highlighting key takeaways such as the superior performance of mT5 with monolingual training over multilingual counterparts. Despite improvements, significant performance gaps persist between monolingual and cross-lingual training methods, underscoring areas needing further research and development to enhance real-world applicability of AI systems in multilingual contexts.

This presentation aims to provide a thorough overview of the advancements and remaining challenges in the field of cross-lingual semantic parsing using large language models, supported by quantitative data and qualitative insights drawn from empirical evaluations and theoretical frameworks.

The slide titled 'Language Modeling' provides a detailed comparison of various pre-training strategies and their performance on different datasets. It includes tables comparing the results from models like CamemBERT, NACHOS, and others across multiple tasks such as Clinical NER, Medical NER, and more. The text explains that DrBERT achieves state-of-the-art results in 9 downstream French medical-oriented tasks, surpasses generic and English-based domain-specific models, confirms the utility of training a medical-specific model in French, emphasizes the importance of data sources, discusses the scalability issues with general data sets versus private clinical data only, highlights the effectiveness of continual pretraining for specific tasks, and notes that all models are freely available under the MIT license.

The slide titled 'Revisiting Minimal Pair Paradigm' discusses the robustness of minimal pair evaluations in language model acceptability judgments. It highlights that these evaluations are sensitive to context length, structural match, and acceptability. The text explains that matched sentences raise or lower judgment performance depending on their structure, with specific examples provided for each category (e.g., "Prefix/suffix adverbs," "Long prefixes," "Add clause," etc.). A graph shows how prefix type affects accuracy across different lengths of input tokens.

The next section is labeled 'Why do matched prefixes affect LM judgements?' This part delves into why matched prefixes impact language model judgments by examining perturbed sentences. Examples include: "What could Jessica before seeing the spotlights?" and "Who had seen the spotlights?" along with a question about Aaron's actions regarding cleaning the museum. Another example asks what Jessica would see before returning from running errands. These questions illustrate how matched prefixes influence LMs' abstract knowledge. The final point emphasizes that models are sensitive to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences, indicating that MPP evaluations with short, single-sentence inputs may not fully capture LMs' abstract knowledge.

The key takeaways reiterate that language models are sensitive to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences and highlight limitations in evaluating LMs' abstract knowledge through short, single-sentence inputs.

The video begins with a title slide that reads 'Minding Language Models' and introduces the topic of measuring Theory of Mind (ToM) in language models. It explains how ToM is traditionally measured using reading comprehension tasks involving multiple characters, such as Alice and Bob, who have different beliefs about each other's knowledge. The presentation delves into the challenges faced by large language models like GPT-3 when reasoning about false-belief scenarios.

The narrative then shifts to discussing SymbolicToM, an inference-time method designed to improve theory-of-mind skills in large language models. This section highlights the benefits of using explicit graphical representations for more interpretable reasoning and emphasizes the improvements made through SymbolicToM compared to traditional supervised approaches.

The next segment focuses on out-of-the-box performance metrics, presenting tables comparing various models across three datasets: Macaw-3B, Flan-T5-XL, Flan-T5-XXL, GPT3-Davinci, LLaMA-7B, and LLaMA-13B. These comparisons are based on QOD story understanding and ParaphrasedToMi dataset scores, showcasing the superior performance of these models over others.

The conclusion reiterates the advantages of SymbolicToM, emphasizing its ability to dramatically enhance out-of-the-box LL defense against attacks while maintaining robustness in linguistic generalization. Specific details include the model's outperformance in OOD story understanding and its effectiveness on the new linguistic diversity dataset ParaphrasedToMi.

The video presents a detailed analysis of the performance and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in constrained language planning tasks, focusing on how these models can generate scripts with specific goals and constraints. It emphasizes the importance of symbolic knowledge distillation for improving LLMs' ability to handle complex scenarios effectively.

The presentation begins by introducing the topic "Constrained Language Planning" and highlights that while LLMs are powerful tools for natural language understanding, they often struggle with decomposing abstract goals into concrete steps due to their inability to reason about actions or infer causality from text. The slide then introduces the concept of script distillation as a method to address this limitation, showing examples like making a cake for different occasions such as weddings, birthdays, and picnics.

The next section details the process of generating specific goals using InstructGPT via in-context learning, over-generating candidate scripts, filtering them based on constraints, and annotating validation sets. This is followed by an evaluation framework involving metrics like ROUGE, BLEU, and BERTScore to assess the quality of generated scripts.

The subsequent slides discuss the limitations and future work related to improving LLMsodels through post-hoc re-ranking approaches. It mentions CoScript as a dataset used for evaluating and developing LLMs capable of handling more complex and multi-faceted goal specifications. The final part of the presentation summarizes key takeaways, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive datasets and advanced research methodologies to enhance the overall effectiveness of LLMsodels in real-world applications.

The slide titled 'Revisiting Minimal Pair Paradigm' focuses on evaluating minimal pairs of sentences with different structures to determine their acceptability and robustness. It includes a detailed explanation of the approach, highlighting that matched MPP sentences raise or lower judgment performance due to their structural matches and semantic meanings. The slide also features examples such as "A rose was in the vase," "There are two roses in the vase," and "There were three roses in the vase." Additionally, it discusses how certain prefixes affect model performances and presents graphs showing the impact of these factors on language model judgments.

The presentation focuses on the analysis of multilingual training, highlighting that mT5 with monolingual training yields the best performance and discussing the challenges faced by multilingual LLMs. It emphasizes the significant gap in performance between monolingual training and cross-lingual transfer learning. The slide also mentions that FunQL outperforms other models but still faces limitations.

The next part transitions to a conclusion section, summarizing key points about XSemPLR as a unified benchmark for cross-lingual semantic parsing and mentioning comprehensive benchmarks conducted on three representative types of language models. It highlights the findings from experiments showing that mT5 with monolingual training performs well compared to other models like mT4, mT3, and mT2. The final slides provide links to access the paper and code related to the project.

The video begins with a title slide displaying the Google Research logo and the text 'Resolving Indirect Referring Expressions for Entity Selection (AltEntities Corpus).' It introduces Mohammad Javad Hosseini, a researcher from Google Research. The presentation is about understanding conversational systems' ability to resolve indirect referring expressions in alternative question pairs by collecting large amounts of data through crowd-sourcing tasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk.

The first section titled 'Dataset Collection Methodology' explains that annotators are asked to generate alternative questions based on given sentences or descriptions. Examples include 'Do you mean A or B?' with options like 'Easy on Me' by Adele and 'I Gotta Feeling' by The Black Eyed Peas. The methodology emphasizes informality using cartoon completion tasks and provides examples such as 'Simnel Cake,' which has layers similar to marzipan but made of almond paste, and 'Pandan Cake,' known for its green color due to pandanus leaves.

The second section focuses on background knowledge required for entity selection. It details how models can handle different levels of access to entities: 92-95% accuracy when LM has full access, 82-87% when it has partial overlap, and 60-65% when it only accesses entity names. The dataset link provided is 'https://github.com/google-research/datasets/AltEntities.'

The third section discusses resolving indirect referents without direct mentions. It shows an example where the speaker asks if they should go see "The Man" instead of "Man of Wood." The model's performance varies depending on the level of access to entities, highlighting domain-generalizability and providing more specific examples related to music and recipes.

The final part includes a thank you message and contact information for Mohammad Javad Hosseini, emphasizing his role at Google Research and inviting further inquiries via email. The overall theme revolves around improving conversational AI through extensive dataset collection and annotation methodologies.

The presentation slide titled 'Experimental Results' discusses the importance of example quality over similarity to source sentences, highlights that specialized SOTA systems have a significant advantage, and notes that PaLM closely matches Google Translate. It also mentions insights from MQM, stating that fluency of PaLM is comparable to SOTA but accuracy scores are generally lower due to issues like "Accuracy/Omission," while style/awkwardness tends to be better for PaLM compared to SOTA. The next section of the presentation addresses the causes of performance drop in named entity recognition (NER) tasks. It lists three main factors contributing to this issue: 'Temporal drift,' 'Not adaptive overfitting,' and 'More fine-tuning examples needed.' These points suggest potential reasons for why NER models may not perform as well on new data or when applied to different datasets.

The subsequent part discusses whether CoNLL-2003 taggers still work effectively today. This question implies an evaluation of the relevance and effectiveness of older tagging methods in contemporary contexts.

The video begins with a slide titled 'From Pretraining Data to Downstream Tasks,' which transitions into an analysis of the political leanings in language models. It highlights how pretraining data from sources like Reddit and news media influences these models, leading to biased performance on downstream tasks such as hate speech detection and misinformation classification. The presentation delves deeper into evaluating these biases using metrics like F1 scores for different categories (news left, news center, news right) across various datasets (Reddit, CNN, Guard, Fox, Breitbart, Washington Post, New York Times). The discussion emphasizes the importance of understanding and addressing these biases through qualitative analyses, showing examples where certain texts are classified differently based on their perceived political leaning by the model. A diagram illustrates the flow from pretraining data to language models and then to downstream tasks, underscoring the need for careful consideration when sanitizing or not sanitizing training data to avoid bias. The narrative continues with a focus on the qualitative analysis section, highlighting specific text examples that demonstrate varying classifications due to political biases. Texts include statements about McDonald's policy changes, the President's response to police brutality, and discussions around COVID-19 vaccines, showcasing diverse perspectives influenced by the model's political leanings. The final segment reiterates the question of whether to sanitize or not to sanitize training data to mitigate unfairness, concluding with a detailed examination of the impact of pretraining data on language model performance and its implications for downstream tasks.

The video presents a comprehensive overview of cognitive dissonance, its effects on disagreement and belief trends, and strategies for annotating rare classes in machine learning. It emphasizes the importance of transfer learning and active learning techniques to improve model performance and efficiency.\n\nThe presentation concludes with contact information for further inquiries, including email addresses and GitHub links, followed by a 'Thank you!' message, indicating the end of the session or lecture.

The video begins with a slide titled 'Prompting PaLM for Translation' from the ACL 2023 conference, presented by Google. It introduces the topic of evaluating the PaLM language model's translation capabilities using various test sets and metrics. The presentation highlights that example quality is more important than similarity to source sentences, specialized SOTA systems have significant advantages, and PaLM performs closely to Google Translate in terms of fluency but generally scores lower on accuracy due to issues like "Accuracy/Omission" and style/awkwardness challenges.
The narrative continues with detailed insights into these findings, emphasizing the importance of example quality over sentence similarity and the relative performance of PaLM compared to other models. Specific attention is given to how PaLM struggles with maintaining high accuracy across different benchmarks, particularly those dominated by tasks requiring precision such as "Accuracy/Omission."
The discussion then shifts focus towards an illustrative segment featuring multilingual expressions of gratitude ("thank you") written in various languages around the central phrase. This visual representation underscores the diversity of global communication practices and serves as a concluding note or transition point within the broader context of the presentation.
Throughout the sequence, the consistent branding elements, including the Google logo and the presenter's image at the bottom right corner, reinforce the professional setting and the authoritative nature of the information being shared.

The presentation slide titled 'Marked Words' is displayed, emphasizing the importance of marked words in evaluating stereotypes. The text reads: 'Marked Words: Find words that distinguish personas of marked groups from unmarked groups.' Examples include 'Vibrant, curvaceous for Latina women,' 'Petite, delicate, silky for Asian women,' and 'Strong, resilient for Black women.'

The slide titled 'How LLMs Perform on Constrained Language Planning' presents a bar chart comparing the accuracy of different models. The bars represent: T5 (175B) with an accuracy slightly above 20, Codex (175B) around 38, InstructGPT (175B) at approximately 46, and T5 trained on wikiHow near 50. The highest bar is for InstructGPT trained on Coscript Dataset, reaching about 59. Below this section, there's another heading labeled 'Script Distillation from LLMs,' which includes detailed information about the method used to improve language planning ability by generating high-quality script datasets ('Coscript Dataset') through in-context learning. It mentions that smaller LM fine-tuned on Coscript can generate higher quality scripts than larger LLMs.

The next part of the presentation focuses on 'Script Distillation from LLMs.' This segment explains how to establish the constrained language planning problem using in-context learning methods like Coscript. It emphasizes evaluating the language planning ability of large language models (LLMs) by over-generating and filtering these models. A specific example shows how to use Coscript to generate high-quality script datasets for constrained language planning. The text highlights that Coscript can inherit only one extra constraint from the abstract one it inherits, making it suitable for improving the performance of smaller LLMs when combined with more complex goals and constraints. The slide also notes that Coscript datasets are valuable resources for advancing research on language planning with more summary and complex goals and constraints.

Following this, the slide transitions into 'Summary and Takeaways.' Here, key points include establishing the constrained language planning problem, evaluating the ability of LLMs, developing an over-generate-then-filter approach for LLMs, and utilizing Coscript to generate high-quality script datasets. The final point discusses limitations and future work, emphasizing that the proposed method improves LLMs as a post-hoc re-ranking approach. It further elaborates on Coscript's capability to inherit only one extra constraint and its value as a resource for advanced research in language planning with more complex goals and constraints.

The last part of the presentation features a slide titled 'Limitations and Future Work.' This section outlines several challenges faced during the study, including issues related to training data size, model capacity, evaluation metrics, and dataset construction. Despite these difficulties, the overall goal was achieved due to the team's hard work and dedication. Additionally, it provides contact details such as a GitHub link (https://github.com/siyuyuan/coscript) and an email address (siyuyuan21@m.fudan.edu.cn). The background image remains consistent throughout, showing a modern office setting with desks, chairs, and people working.

The slide titled 'Constrained Language Planning' discusses the challenges of achieving high-quality scripts with specific goals and constraints. The subsequent sections include 'Method,' detailing the approach used to improve LLMs through symbolic knowledge distillation, and 'Limitations and Future Work,' discussing the proposed method as a post-hoc re-ranking approach and highlighting issues like Coscript's single extra constraint and its value as a resource for advanced research. The fourth slide delves into the specifics of the evaluation metric R-Precision (R-prec), defined as the ratio of the number of correct predictions over the total predicted set size. It uses the formula R-prec = (#(top-R important words / Annotated words) / |I|. Here, I represents the index set containing all annotated sentences. The slide emphasizes the precision criterion used to measure the accuracy of identifying relevant keywords or segments from annotated financial reports. The explanation clarifies why this metric ensures only top-R most informative tokens are considered, thereby maintaining relevance while filtering out less critical pieces of information.

The fifth slide extends the previous discussions on evaluation metrics by introducing P-R Precision (P-prec), another essential component of the evaluation strategy. P-prec is calculated as P-prec = (#(highlighted words / Total highlighted words) / (#(highlighted words / Annotated words). Unlike R-prec, P-prec considers the proportion of correctly highlighted words among those marked up by annotators. This metric helps assess the consistency and comprehensiveness of the highlighting task, ensuring that a larger portion of the highlighted sections accurately reflects the actual annotations made by experts. The slide reinforces the dual-purpose nature of these metrics—R-prec evaluates overall prediction accuracy, whereas P-prec checks for completeness and alignment with expert annotations.

The slide titled 'Pangu Framework' introduces the Pangu framework, which aims to improve grounded language understanding by allowing large language models (LLMs) to focus on discrimination tasks. It emphasizes that LLMs are generic and highlights two key goals: 1. Allowing LLMs to focus on discrimination, and 2. Being generic. The presentation includes a detailed discussion of these objectives through various slides, such as one showing a neural agent interacting with an environment and proposing valid candidate plans, another discussing the challenges faced during training, and multiple comparisons between different models like ArcaneQA, Pangu (BERT-base), and Pangu (T5-base). The findings section notes improvements in sample efficiency for generating text data compared to other methods. Additionally, there is a comparison chart illustrating differences in performance across various datasets, including GrailQA, WebQSP, and WebSP, highlighting how each model performs under different conditions. The final sections emphasize the importance of addressing biases in AI systems and provide visual aids to illustrate concepts related to generation and discrimination tasks within the context of using large language models for grounded language understanding.

The slide titled 'Background' provides an overview of the research context, highlighting large language models (LLMs) like GPT [1], LLAMA [2], and PALM [3] that are exceptional in natural language understanding tasks but pose challenges for copyright protection. It introduces EmbMarker as a solution to protect intellectual property by embedding backdoors into EaaS services while maintaining utility and security.

The section on 'Watermark injection' details how the watermark is integrated with the target embedding using a backdoor weight, ensuring it does not degrade performance or privacy. The process involves copying datasets from AG News, MIND, Enron Spam, and WikiText, verifying extracted embeddings against the provider's service, and comparing detection metrics across different methods.

The 'Experimental Results' segment presents tables summarizing accuracy and detection performance metrics for various datasets and methods, including original, RedAlarm, EmbMarker, and Ours. It also includes visualizations of embeddings for four datasets: AG News, Enron Spam, MIND, and SST2, demonstrating the distribution of data points in two-dimensional space.

Finally, the presentation concludes with a simple white background displaying the text 'Thanks!' indicating the end of the presentation.

The presentation slide titled 'KITMUS Test Suite' introduces the evaluation of NLU models using a dataset from the KITMUS project. It emphasizes that these models are designed to integrate pretrain-time knowledge and inference-time context, which is essential for understanding information in natural language text. The slide highlights the importance of testing how well these models can handle complex tasks by drawing on multiple sources of background knowledge.

The slide features an illustration depicting two people named John and Kea, who work at different companies (a law firm and a bakery). A fictional scenario describes their meeting over coffee after working long hours. This setup illustrates the challenges faced by modern AI systems when integrating various types of contextual knowledge into their decision-making processes.

The slide also includes references to academic papers such as 'How do neural networks reason about entities?' by Yoon et al., 2018; 'How do neural networks understand temporal relations?' by Park et al., 2019; and 'How does a neural network solve the problem of entity grounding?' by Kim et al., 2019. These references underscore the complexity involved in developing AI models capable of comprehending and reasoning with diverse forms of textual data.

Throughout the presentation, the focus remains on demonstrating the limitations of current AI models in handling multifaceted scenarios where they must combine both pretrain-time and inference-time knowledge to make accurate decisions or predictions based on given contexts.

The slide titled 'MeetingBank: A Benchmark Dataset for Meeting Summarization' introduces the dataset, highlighting its creation through segmenting city council meetings and pairing them with expert-written summaries. It emphasizes that this dataset is a valuable resource for researchers developing advanced meeting summarizers and provides insights into the decision-making process of city councils.

The presentation continues to detail the contributions from various contributors such as Yelowen Ha, Tim Gartner, Haisheh Delimahmoudy, Fransc Droncomcourt, Hassan Frousoei, and Li Wei. The logos of Adobe Research, Emory University, and Emory University Library are displayed at the bottom right corner throughout the slides.

The presentation slide titled 'Prompting PaLM for Translation' provides a detailed overview of the study's methodology, findings, and experimental results. The text emphasizes that WSL approaches benefit from more clean validation samples and suggests applying continuous fine-tuning (CFT) instead of using weakly labeled training data.

The slide titled 'ABC-Eval Behaviors' features a chart comparing the error rates of various models, including BART-FID-RAG, Blender2, Emora, and Blender-Decode. The x-axis lists different categories such as 'Asocial,' 'CS Contra,' 'Ignore,' etc., while the y-axis shows the percentage of turns with errors. Each model's performance is represented by bars in blue (BART-FID-RAG), purple (Blender2), green (Emora), and red (Blender-Decode). The slide titled 'NLP' presents a framework for understanding the positionality of NLP datasets and models. It includes sections on 'Annotator Positionality,' 'Model Positionality,' and 'Dataset Positionality.' The text explains that annotators have diverse backgrounds, with 58% being female, 42% male, and representing over 100 countries worldwide.

The slide titled 'KITMUS Test Suite' introduces the KITMUS test suite, which is designed to evaluate a model's ability to integrate pretrain-time and inference-time knowledge. It highlights that many models struggle with this task due to the lack of integration between these two types of knowledge. The slide also mentions that entity-specific training can help improve performance in tasks involving background knowledge from multiple sources.

The title of the presentation is 'A Needle in a Haystack: An Analysis of High-Agreement Workers on MTurk.' The slide outlines two main pipelines for finding high-agreement workers on MTurk, detailing the qualification and endurance tasks involved. It highlights that 200 workers were filtered out, resulting in four gold (high agreement) and eight silver (high agreement but with some errors) workers. These findings are presented as best practices to achieve high agreement at scale while minimizing resource waste and avoiding annotation biases. The future applications include multiple task types, languages, platforms, etc., aiming to maintain or improve worker quality through better annotation processes.

The next section discusses limitations related to the reference-based task used in the study. It mentions issues such as English summarization problems, designed questions not being panaceas, no guarantee for the training of correctness, and Spearman's correlation between MTurk workers' performance and expert judgments. Despite these challenges, the study achieved high agreement among annotators using CloudResearch tools like Google Forms and Excel. The pipeline consisted of three phases: qualification, endurance, and annotation feedback, involving over 150 unique MTurk workers across various studies. The results showed significant improvement from previous work, achieving higher levels of agreement than earlier studies.

The final part presents an analysis of correctness across annotation sources, showing a strong Spearman correlation between MTurk workers' performances and expert judgments. This indicates reliable annotation outcomes despite initial concerns about MTurk workers' ability to perform well. The discussion emphasizes the need for further research into how to train MTurk workers effectively to ensure consistent high-quality annotations.

The conclusion reiterates the success of filtering out low-performing workers and maintaining high agreement rates among those remaining. It underscores the importance of this approach in improving annotation accuracy and efficiency. The acknowledgments note support from NYU, GEM, and Google for funding the experiment.

The detailed steps outlined involve pre-defined qualifications, including evaluation criteria based on attention check scores, summary evaluations, and candidate summaries. The design choices aimed to reduce noise and enhance annotation quality. The baseline filter included specific conditions such as completing all documents within one hour without any errors, having a maximum of five errors per document, and passing attention checks. The end-of-task questionnaire ensured thorough evaluation before moving forward to the endurance phase.

The endurance task required workers to complete additional tasks under strict time constraints, ensuring they maintained their focus and productivity throughout. The process culminated in a two-step annotation feedback mechanism where workers reviewed annotated data and provided ratings, which influenced subsequent assignments. This method helped identify consistently high-performing workers who could be retained for more complex tasks.

The overall strategy focused on optimizing the selection and retention of highly competent workers by systematically removing those unable to meet stringent standards, thereby enhancing the reliability and consistency of the annotation outputs.

The presentation slide titled 'FactKG: Fact Verification via Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs' introduces the concept of using knowledge graphs for fact verification. It highlights that a KG is used as evidence to support claims, with examples like 'AIDAstella was built by Meyer Werft.' The slide emphasizes the reliability and practicality of this approach.

The next section focuses on five types of reasoning: One-hop, Conjuction, Existence, Multi-hop, and Negation. Each type includes specific claim examples and corresponding graph representations. For instance, under 'One-hop,' it shows 'AIDAstella was built by Meyer Werft,' illustrating how entities are connected through one relation.

The slide then delves into the process of verifying facts through multi-hop inference when some entities do not appear in the original claim but can be inferred from existing data. This involves converting claims only or adding evidence to form more complex queries.

The detailed table at the bottom lists various models (BERT, BlueBERT, Flan-T5, and GEAR) along with their performance accuracy across different types of reasoning tasks such as One-hop, Conjuction, Existence, Multi-hop, and Negation. The slide titled 'Revisiting Minimal Pair Paradigm' focuses on evaluating Minimal Pairs (MPP) in different contexts. It highlights the importance of context length, structural match, and acceptability in language model judgments. The text explains that MPP evaluations with short, single-sentence inputs do not fully capture language models' abstract knowledge. Examples include sentences like "Many people were helping" versus "No customer had a ticket," showing how these minimal pairs affect judgment performance. A graph illustrates the relationship between prefix type and accuracy across various perturbations. Key takeaways emphasize that language models are sensitive to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences and that MPP evaluations need longer inputs for accurate results.

The presentation slide titled 'DisorBERT' introduces a new model designed to adapt BERT for mental disorder detection. It features the text 'DisorBERT' in large, bold letters with an orange background and includes two sections: 'BERT' on the left and 'DisorBERT' on the right. The next section provides detailed information about the DisorBERT model's development process. It explains that the combined effect of domain adaptation and guided masking was effective in capturing signs of mental disorders from social media interactions. The approach resulted in better performance than MentalBERT, which used larger amounts of data but consumed more computational resources. A solid balance between finding users and labeling them correctly made DisorBERT suitable for clinical detection applications. Future work aims to explore different lexical resources and usage of clinical data to train specialized language models.

Each plot uses color-coded markers representing different methods like BERT, RoBERTa, XLM-Glue, MentaBERT, RoBERTa-SVM, DisorBERT, and PNN-Glue. The plots illustrate how these methods perform under varying conditions.

The final segment presents conclusions and future work related to the study. The presentation slide titled 'Uncertainty Estimation' focuses on the importance of uncertainty estimation in document-level relation extraction. It introduces a dynamic class uncertainty threshold strategy to filter high-uncertainty pseudo labels, highlighting its application and effectiveness through detailed explanations and mathematical equations.

The slide transitions into discussing the proposed framework for document-level distant extraction with uncertainty-guided label denoising, emphasizing improvements over existing baselines using experimental data from two datasets: DocRED and Re-DocRED. The performance metrics such as F1 score, Ignorance F1 (Ign F1), and Average Precision at different thresholds are provided, showcasing significant improvements achieved by the new approach.

The final part of the presentation provides an overview of the conclusion section, summarizing key points about the novel instance-level uncertainty estimation method, iterative re-labeling strategy, and overall performance improvements. Experimental results illustrate the enhanced baseline performances when trained on denoised DS (Distant Supervision) data.

The video concludes with a thank you message, expressing gratitude to the audience for watching, followed by logos of various institutions involved in the research or collaboration, including the University of Science and Technology of China, DeClaRe, and SUTD (Singapore University of Technology and Design).

The slide titled 'Experimental Results' provides a detailed analysis of the findings from MQM. The key points include: 1. Example quality is more important than similarity to source sentence, which affects accuracy scores and fluency metrics. 2. Specialized SOTA systems have a significant advantage in terms of accuracy scores. 3. PaLM closely matches Google Translate's performance. Insights from MQM indicate that while PaLM has comparable fluency to SOTA, its accuracy scores are generally lower due to challenges with "Accuracy/Omission" tasks. Additionally, there are issues related to style and awkwardness for PaLM when translating into German.

The slide titled 'Background' introduces the concept of watermarking in large language models (LLMs) and embedding-based services. It explains how to define a target embedding, count trigger words within sentences, add them to the original embedding, normalize it, and compare it with the provider's EaaS embeddings using metrics like cosine similarity (\(\Delta_{cos}\)) and p-value for detection performance.

The video presentation is titled 'Transfer and Active Learning for Annotating Rare Classes' by Vasudha Varadarajan, presented at the 2019 Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL). Further slides provide detailed explanations of various active learning strategies, including PRC (Probability of Rare Class), which simplifies and improves sample acquisition for rare classes. The presentation includes diagrams showing iterative versus cumulative training processes and discusses the benefits of each strategy. The final segment lists key takeaways about cold-start active learning, transfer learning, and iterative vs. cumulative strategies. It concludes with contact information for further inquiries and references to related papers and datasets available online.

The slide titled 'Revisiting Minimal Pair Paradigm' introduces the concept of minimal pair evaluations in sequence probabilities (P(LM)) and evaluates MPP sentences with different structures. It discusses how these evaluations affect model performance, emphasizing that acceptable/unacceptable judgments are robust for arbitrary context lengths but most severely affected by matched structure sentences.

The next section explains why matched prefixes affect LM judgements, highlighting that models are sensitive to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences. The evaluation method is described as not fully capturing LMs' abstract knowledge when using short, single-sentence inputs.

A key takeaway emphasizes that language models are sensitive to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences. Additionally, it notes that MPP evaluations do not capture LMs' abstract knowledge well due to their reliance on short, single-sentence inputs.

The final part of the presentation focuses on a specific example where text utterances contain matched prefixes, showing how this affects the judgment outcomes. It includes examples from 'BLIMP' and 'Wiki' datasets, illustrating the impact of matched prefixes on sentence acceptability judgments.

The detailed explanation provided covers the methodology behind evaluating MPP sentences, the sensitivity of language models to shared syntactic/semantic features, and the limitations of current evaluation methods. This comprehensive overview aims to enhance understanding of how contextualized language model evaluations can better reflect underlying linguistic patterns and improve overall model performance.

The slide titled 'Challenges with Existing Approaches' discusses the limitations of existing approaches in emotion recognition tasks. It highlights issues such as the lack of correlation between textual, audio, and visual modalities for most emotions except anger, which is well correlated across all three modalities. The text emphasizes that these correlations are not observed for other emotions like happiness or sadness. Additionally, it mentions the difficulty in distinguishing between speakers and irrelevant people in scenes using VisNet.

The next section, 'Challenges with Existing Approaches,' elaborates on specific challenges faced by current methods. These include the inability to distinguish between different speakers and irrelevant individuals in a scene due to the use of VisNet. Furthermore, there is an imbalance issue within MELD, where the SWFC loss requires a large batch size to ensure at least one positive pair per training sample, making computational expenses high. Despite achieving improvements in minority emotion categories, MultiEMO's performance remains worse than majority classes in those areas.

The final part of the presentation addresses the 'Limitations.' This segment lists several points about the limitations encountered during the study. One key point is that VisNet does not differentiate between various speakers and irrelevant people in the scene. Another limitation mentioned is the class imbalance problem associated with MELD, leading to the requirement of a large batch size to prevent any negative pairs from appearing in each training sample, resulting in significant computational costs. Lastly, even though MultiEMO has made notable advancements in improving performances in minority emotion categories compared to previous models, its overall performance still lags behind when dealing with minority emotions versus majority ones.

The slide concludes with a detailed explanation of how these limitations impact the effectiveness and efficiency of existing emotional recognition systems, emphasizing the need for more robust and efficient methodologies to address these challenges comprehensively.

The slide then transitions into a new topic: 'Case Study - Emotion Recognition Challenges in Conversational Speech.' This case study focuses on the difficulties encountered while recognizing emotions based solely on conversational speech. A figure illustrates this challenge through a flowchart showing the process of integrating multimodal cues (textual, audio, and visual) to capture the complexity of human emotions. The example provided involves analyzing the utterance 'Chandler is a great name!' spoken by Phoebe, who expresses anger. The chart details how context modeling and multimodal fusion help mitigate the synchronization errors among different modalities, highlighting the importance of accurately capturing both textual and audio-visual information to improve the accuracy of emotion recognition.

The slide continues with a detailed breakdown of the process:
1. **Context Modeling:** - Textual, Audio, and Visual modalities are integrated. - Example Utterance: "Chandler is a great name!" - Speaker: Phoebe - Emotion: Anger
2. **Multimodal Fusion:** - The system uses stacked bidirectional cross-attention layers to fuse the modalities.
3. **Visualization of Heatmaps:** - The heatmaps illustrate the alignment of textual, audio, and visual data. - Example: Phoebe's utterance shows how her words align with her facial expressions and tone to convey anger.
4. **Flowchart Explanation:** - The flowchart visually represents the integration process: - Textual, Audio, and Visual inputs converge towards a unified representation. - This unified representation helps in accurately identifying the underlying emotion despite potential misalignments or discrepancies in individual modality interpretations.
5. **Example Visualization:** - An image shows Phoebe speaking, with corresponding annotations indicating the alignment of her verbal content ("Chandler is a great name!") with her facial expression and vocal tone. - The visualization demonstrates how the model successfully captures the complex interplay of different modalities to recognize the emotion conveyed.
6. **Conclusion:** - The slide underscores the significance of accurate multimodal cue integration in enhancing the reliability and precision of emotion recognition algorithms, especially in scenarios involving conversational speech where multiple sources of information must be harmonized effectively.
This comprehensive approach ensures that the model can handle the nuances of real-world conversations, providing insights into how modern techniques aim to bridge gaps caused by asynchronous or conflicting signals from different sensory channels.

The slide ends with a summary of the findings and their implications for future research directions in the field of automatic emotion recognition.

The slide titled 'Thematic analysis of high P-CXMI' introduces the Multilingual Discourse-Aware (MuDA) tagger, which is a tool for identifying discourse phenomena. The slide includes an illustration of documents and a robot icon labeled 'MuDA tagger,' emphasizing its role in analyzing text data.

The next section provides detailed results from the MuDA benchmark, highlighting that DeepL outperforms Google on most phenomena and language pairs as of April 2021. It also mentions that context-aware models perform significantly better than traditional models when it comes to ellipsis, pronouns, and verb form.

The final part summarizes key points: identifying discourse phenomena systematically without prior linguistic knowledge and establishing a dataset-agnostic benchmark for document-level machine translation using the MuDA tagger and BLEU COMET F-measure metrics.

The presentation continues with a summary slide focusing on summarizing findings related to identifying discourse phenomena systematically without prior linguistic knowledge and establishing a dataset-agnostic benchmark for document-level machine translation. The slide features illustrations representing various stages of the process, including the MuDA tagger, BLEU COMET F-measure calculation, and model evaluation.

The consistent visual elements include icons such as stacked papers, a robot head, and speech bubbles indicating different aspects of the research or methodology being discussed. The background remains plain white throughout these slides, maintaining focus on the textual content and graphical representations.

The overall structure emphasizes clarity and simplicity, ensuring that viewers can easily follow along with the explanations provided by Patrick Fernandes and Kaylene Liu.

The presentation slide titled 'Problem Statement' introduces the challenge of transferring author styles in stories while preserving content. It highlights two main challenges: 1) Imitating the linguistic choices made by a specific author, and 2) Preserving the original story's meaning without altering its core narrative or plot. The slide emphasizes that these tasks are distinct from traditional machine translation problems.

The solution section outlines a framework for addressing these issues through discourse representation transfer and style-specific enhancement. This involves masking source texts to embed them into transferred stories and training an encoder-decoder model with attention mechanisms to reconstruct masked sentences accurately. The approach aims to achieve high-quality translations that capture both stylistic nuances and factual details.

The detailed explanation includes diagrams illustrating data preprocessing steps, such as identifying Chinese-style contents within English text paragraphs using regular expressions. These steps help extract relevant segments for further processing. The diagram also shows how the model processes input sequences (x) to generate output sequences (y), incorporating attention mechanisms to focus on important parts of the input during decoding.

A table summarizes ablation study results on the Chinese-English (CH-EN) dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of different components like the masker, attention mechanism, and decoder. The findings indicate improvements when removing individual components sequentially, highlighting their contributions to the overall performance of the model.

The case study section provides examples comparing the generated translated texts with those produced by JieYan and StoryYuan models, showcasing differences in style preservation and accuracy across various test sets. The comparison illustrates how Xuekai Zhu's proposed method handles complex scenarios involving multiple characters and settings more effectively than existing approaches.

The final slides include contact information for Xuekai Zhu and a thank you message, emphasizing gratitude towards collaborators and supporters.

The video presents a detailed discussion on the dependency structure of coordination in English, focusing on various syntactic structures and their compatibility with different dependency length minimization (DLM) strategies. It begins by introducing the concept of conjunct lengths in English and transitions to explaining the dependency length minimization process using visual aids such as diagrams and graphs. The presentation covers topics like left and right conjunctions, governor positions, and the impact of these factors on dependency length differences. Specific examples are provided to illustrate how conjunctions affect sentence structure and word order.

The slide titled 'Dependency Length Minimization' explains that left conjunctions tend to be shorter than right conjunctions due to a tendency for the governor to appear on the left side of the conjunction. This is supported by statistical data from Gibson et al., 1996, which shows an average difference of around -20 words between left and right conjunctions. Examples demonstrate sentences where Homer loves Lisa, Bart, and Maggie, highlighting the dependency length differences based on whether the governor appears on the left or right.

Further slides delve into the compatibility of different dependency structures with DLM, showing diagrams of sentences and indicating whether they meet certain criteria. For instance, it compares Bouquet/Stanford (Universal Dependencies), Chain/Moscow, Conjunction-headed/Prague, and Multi-headed/London, providing green check marks or red crosses to indicate compliance. Sentences like 'Homer loves Lisa, Bart, and Maggie.' are used to exemplify each case study.

The final part of the presentation includes a call to action, encouraging viewers to see the paper for more details and suggesting discussions at a poster session. The text reads: 'See the paper for the full argument!' and 'Talk to us at the poster session!' emphasizing the importance of consulting the referenced materials for comprehensive insights.

Overall, the video provides a thorough exploration of the complexities involved in understanding and managing dependency lengths in linguistic structures within the context of conjunctions and coordination in English.

The slide titled 'FSUIE: A Novel Fuzzy Span Loss' introduces a method for enhancing Universal Information Extraction (UIE) by focusing on global features and fuzzy span attention. It highlights the benefits of using global features to capture more information from context, which is crucial in natural language processing tasks like Named Entity Recognition (NER). The slide emphasizes that FSUIE aims to improve UIE performance through adaptive adjustment of the attention span within local contexts.

The next section, 'FSUIE utilizes efficient Fuzzy Span Attention,' explains how FSUIE adjusts the distribution of attention based on the length of preceding tokens, leading to better results across various information extraction tasks such as NER, Relation Extraction (RE), and Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ASTE).

The final part of the presentation focuses on the conclusion, summarizing key points about FSUIE's novel loss function, its efficiency in handling span boundaries, and its superior performance compared to existing models. This includes specific improvements in precision, recall, and f1 scores across different datasets and tasks.

The concluding slides emphasize the effectiveness of FSUIE in improving model robustness against adversarial attacks and achieving high accuracy rates in various evaluation metrics. They highlight the advantages of FSUIE over other state-of-the-art methods, showcasing significant improvements in P, R, and F1 scores for both ACE04 and ACE05 datasets.

The detailed analysis demonstrates FSUIE's ability to generalize well across multiple datasets, including ACE03, ACE04, ACE05, and RE, with notable improvements in all evaluated categories. The presentation concludes by reinforcing the superiority of FSUIE in terms of adaptability, generalization capability, and overall performance enhancement in diverse information extraction scenarios.

The visualizations presented include heatmaps showing attention distributions, illustrating how FSUIE adapts attention spans effectively. These visuals help explain the mechanism behind FSUIE's enhanced performance, providing a comprehensive understanding of its contributions to the field of natural language processing.

The consistent use of logos throughout the slides reinforces the branding of Wuhan University and Shangai Jiao Tong University, emphasizing their involvement in this research project.

Overall, the presentation provides a thorough overview of FSUIE's methodology, benefits, and empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness in advancing UIE capabilities.

The slide includes a graph showing the impact on model performance, highlighting specific examples such as "There was a documentary about music," "What could Jessica before seeing it?" and "Who might Rose from this customer before returning to this customer?". The final part focuses on the sensitivity of language models to latent syntactic/semantic features shared across sentences. The slide titled 'DrBERT: A French pre-trained model for biomedical tasks' introduces the DrBERT model, which is a robust and effective tool in the field of natural language processing (NLP) within the medical domain. It highlights that DrBERT surpasses other models like CamemBERT and generic English-based models by achieving state-of-the-art results on 9 downstream French medical-oriented tasks. The presentation emphasizes the importance of training based on heterogeneous data sources rather than private clinical data only to ensure better performance. Additionally, it mentions that NACHOS is more robust with heterogeneous data but does not scale well. Furthermore, continual pretraining proves to be an effective strategy when working with domain-specific English models. The slides also provide information about the availability of the models, datasets, and scripts under MIT licenses through the website 'drbert.univ-avignon.fr'.

The slide titled 'Language Modeling' provides an overview of the evaluation process and compares different models on various tasks. It highlights that DrBERT achieves state-of-the-art results in 9 downstream French medical-oriented tasks, surpasses CamemBERT generic model and English-based domain-specific models, confirms the utility of training a medical-specific model in French, and emphasizes the importance of data sources for heterogeneous data.
The section labeled 'Core message' summarizes key points: - DRBERT's achievements. - Importance of diverse data sources. - Scalability issues with more data. - Advantages of continual pretraining over one-time training. - Availability of resources under MIT license.

The video features a presentation on 'Dependency Length Minimization (DLM)' in English, focusing on the compatibility of conjunction lengths with dependency structures. It begins by explaining how left conjuncts are shorter than right conjuncts when both governors have equal length and discusses various coordination types such as Bouquet/Stanford, Chain/Moscow, Conjunction-headed/Praque, Multi-headed/London, and their respective dependencies. The slide transitions to show different scenarios where conjunction lengths vary based on governor lengths, highlighting that left conjuncts tend to be shorter regardless of whether they appear before or after the governor. The presentation then delves into detailed graphs illustrating the relationship between absolute difference in lengths and the proportion of left conjunct lengths depending on these differences.

The focus shifts to specific examples like 'I saw Bart and Lisa; Homer came and sneezed,' emphasizing the consistency across different contexts. A new section titled 'Compatibility with Dependency Structures of Coordination' appears, categorizing sentences under 'Bouquet/Stanford (Universal Dependencies),' 'Chain/Moscow,' 'Conjunction-headed/Praque,' and 'Multi-headed/London.' Sentences like 'Homer loves Lisa, Bart, and Maggie' illustrate compatibility issues for certain coordination types while confirming others. The final part of the presentation includes slides encouraging viewers to see the paper for more details and inviting them to talk at the poster session. Throughout, the presenter's name is consistently displayed in the top-right corner, maintaining continuity throughout the clips.

The last segment emphasizes the importance of consulting the full paper for comprehensive understanding and engagement during the poster session, reinforcing key points about conjunction lengths and their compatibility with dependency structures.

The slide titled 'MODELLING PERSPECTIVES' introduces a study on the importance of a perspectivist approach for irony detection. It contrasts this with standard non-perspectivist approaches and highlights that perspective-aware models tend to make decisions with less uncertainty, especially when tested on data sets representative of their own perspectives. The text emphasizes that these models are more confident in their predictions compared to those trained without considering self-declared gender or country of residence. A table compares F1-scores from gold test set averages across different model types, showing significant differences between perspectivist-based tests and non-perspectivist ones.

A detailed analysis follows, focusing on how perspective-aware models perform better than standard non-perspectivist models, particularly highlighting variations in Irony Perception (IAA). The presentation includes visual elements such as stick figures illustrations representing different perspectives and annotated instances from various language varieties. The final slides provide insights into the distribution of IAA among different demographics like gender, age group, nationality, ethnicity, student status, employment status, and education level, using violin plots to illustrate the variation in perception scores. These visuals help understand the impact of demographic factors on the interpretation of irony.

The overall message is clear: incorporating diverse perspectives leads to improved accuracy and confidence in detecting irony, which can be crucial for developing effective natural language understanding systems.

The video concludes by emphasizing the significance of varied perspectives in improving ironical detection algorithms, supported by statistical evidence and illustrative diagrams.

The presentation begins with a title slide introducing the topic 'From Dogwhistles to Bullhorns: Evaluating Language Models on Coded Rhetoric,' followed by an overview of dogwhistles and their evolution from coded language to overt expressions. It discusses how these terms are used in political messaging, particularly focusing on historical figures like Josh Hawley who employ them.

The project's goals are outlined next, including creating typologies and glossaries for different types of dogwhistles (racist, antisemitic, transphobic), conducting case studies using historical speeches, evaluating dogwhistle recognition in language models, and demonstrating how dogwhistles can evade content moderation systems. The importance of understanding context and persona in interpreting dogwhistles is emphasized through various examples and explanations.

A detailed analysis follows, showing that GPT-3 surfaces 45% of dogwhistles but only identifies formal group labels when slurs or standard group labels are replaced with dogwhistles. This highlights the challenge of detecting toxicity accurately without proper contextual information. The performance varies significantly across categories such as 'antisemitic' and 'racist,' indicating that dogwhistles may be rated less toxic if they replace traditional slurs or group labels.

The presentation then transitions into practical applications, discussing the use of templates for identifying dogwhistles and the need for rich contextual information. It emphasizes the importance of evaluating dogwhistle recognition in language models and shows how these tools often fail to detect hate speech due to insufficient training data. Examples include terms like 'tax relief' being misclassified as harmless.

The final slides reiterate the objectives of the project, highlighting the creation of typologies and glossaries, evaluation methods, and demonstrations of evasion techniques. They stress the necessity of incorporating diverse contexts and personas to improve detection accuracy, providing visual aids such as icons representing different aspects of the study. The consistent theme throughout all slides is the critical examination of dogwhistles within language models and their implications for content moderation practices.

The video concludes with a comprehensive summary of the project's key points, underscoring the challenges and ongoing efforts to enhance the identification and mitigation of dogwhistles in online discourse.

The slide titled 'Named Entity Recognition & Generalization' introduces the topic with a focus on model architecture, larger model size, and more fine-tuning examples. It questions whether CoNLL-2003 taggers still work in modern contexts.

Next, the slide transitions to discussing performance drop causes, specifically temporal drift and not adaptive overfitting. The text 'Do CoNLL-2003 taggers still work?' is followed by an affirmative answer: 'YES'

The presentation continues with detailed explanations of these factors, emphasizing that while there are issues like temporal drift causing performance degradation, models can adapt better than initially thought. The discussion highlights how time-dependent changes impact NER systems, leading to decreased accuracy due to outdated data or methods.

The Georgia Tech logo remains visible throughout the slides, reinforcing the academic context of the presentation.

The video presents a detailed overview of the research on improving the robustness of NLI models through minimax training, emphasizing the challenges posed by shortcut correlations and introducing an innovative approach to address these issues. It highlights the advantages of this method, such as its ability to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) performance while maintaining high in-domain accuracy. The presentation also includes experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the minimax training strategy across various datasets and model sizes.

The slide titled 'Our approach: minimax training' introduces the main idea behind minimizing the correlation between loss and label for improved generalization. It explains that the learner optimizes the task with minimal loss, while the auxiliary maximizes the loss given the predictions from the example weights. This is visually represented using a flowchart illustrating the interaction between the learner and the auxiliary components.

The discussion then shifts to the impact of pre-training the learner, asking how it affects the overall performance and what size the auxiliary needs to be. These questions are highlighted in red text to emphasize their importance in understanding the proposed methodology further.

The presentation slide titled 'Named Entity Recognition & Generalization' introduces the topic with a focus on evaluating how well models perform in Named Entity Recognition (NER) tasks. The slide transitions into discussing what is needed for good generalization, emphasizing better model architecture, larger model size, more fine-tuning examples, and avoiding performance drop caused by temporal drift or adaptive overfitting. The Georgia Tech logo remains visible throughout, maintaining brand consistency.

The conclusion section reiterates key points about necessary changes for effective NER models, including improving model architecture, increasing model capacity, providing ample training data, and addressing issues related to temporal drift and adaptive overfitting. A specific example shows a significant improvement when transitioning from RoBERTa to Flair models, highlighting the impact of these adjustments on performance.
